newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Bashir to S.Africa for civil war peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Bashir to S.Africa for civil war peace talks.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela was preparing on Monday for delicate talks on ways to end a 14-year civil war in southern Sudan with Sudanese President Omar Hassan al-Bashir, officials said.
Bashir was due to arrive in Pretoria from Khartoum later on Monday. His discussions with Mandela were scheduled to start on Tuesday morning.

Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, who has recently met delegations from the conflicting sides in the Sudan, would also send a special envoy to South Africa to attend the talks, Pretoria's Foreign Affairs Department said in a statement.
The envoy, who was not named, would be at the meeting "in support of finding an acceptable and lasting solution to the problem", the department added, without elaborating.
Mandela has played the role of peace broker several times since he emerged in 1990 from over a quarter-of-a-century in jail to lead South Africa from apartheid to democracy.

Alone or in concert with other southern African leaders, he has contributed to peacemaking missions in Angola, Algeria, Lesotho, Swaziland, Burundi, Nigeria and Zaire, which is now known as the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
In the Sudan, Mandela has attempted over the past few months to help mediate in the fighting which has pitted Christian, animist rebels in the south against the Moslem, Arab north.

Pretoria said Bashir's visit was at Mandela's request and took place against the background of a regional peace initiative under the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), chaired by Kenyan leader Daniel arap Moi.

"President Mandela and the South African government fully support and encourage all parties to the conflict in Sudan to participate constructively in the IGAD initiative," the brief foreign affairs statement said.

John Garang, leader of the rebel Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), has already held talks with Mandela on ways to end the war. Pretoria's Foreign Affairs Department confirmed on Monday that they met in South Africa in December 1996.
